title: who your neighbor turns out to be
hookLine: a good Samaritan on the local news, and who the Samaritans actually were
carry: the neighbor is whoever is in front of you

lines: A GOOD SAMARITAN, ON THE NEWS.
cards: A good Samaritan stops at a car crash, and it's on the local news. There are laws named after the phrase, and hospitals.

Hardly anyone who uses it knows who the Samaritans were, or why, to the first people who heard it, a good Samaritan sounded almost like a contradiction. It starts with a man who knew his Bible very well.
He and Jesus agree on the heart of it: love God with everything, and love your neighbor as yourself. Then the man asks the follow-up everybody quietly wants to ask. "And who is my neighbour?"

teach.b: Jesus answers with a story, in Luke's Gospel. "A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among thieves." They strip him, beat him and leave him half dead in the ditch.
A priest comes down the road, sees him, and passes by on the other side.
Then a Levite, who served in the Temple, does the same. The story never says why. They're characters in a story, not a verdict on anyone's faith; Jesus and the man asking him were Jews too.
Then a third traveler: a Samaritan. Samaritans and Judeans were related peoples who shared the books of Moses, but they worshipped on different mountains and had centuries of bad blood between them.

teach.h: THE ONE FROM ACROSS THE LINE STOPS.
teach.b: So the hero of the story comes from across the line. And he's the one who stops. The old English says "he had compassion on him."

He bandages the wounds, pours in oil and wine, puts the man on his own animal, takes him to an inn, and pays for his stay, with a promise to cover whatever else it costs. Then the twist. The man had asked: who counts?
Jesus turns it around: "Which now of these three, thinkest thou, was neighbour unto him that fell among the thieves?"
Not who qualifies. Who acted like one. The man answers, "He that shewed mercy on him."
And Jesus says: "Go, and do thou likewise."

how: Christians read the Good Samaritan as a picture of what loving your neighbor looks like in practice. Many churches, hospitals and charities are named after it, and many Christians take it as a reason to help strangers in need.

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: passed by on the other side
saw him and passed by too
bandaged him and paid the inn

s: Samaritans and Judeans were long-time friends
they were related neighbors who shared the books of Moses, but worshipped on different mountains and had centuries of bad blood.
the story explains why the priest and the Levite passed by
it doesn't. the text is silent, and people have guessed ever since.
Jesus ends by asking who acted like a neighbor, not who counts as one
he asks which of the three was a neighbor to the man. not who qualifies. who acted.

games.q: you're a Samaritan on the road to Jericho. a stranger from the other side of an old feud is half dead in the ditch. two travelers have already passed. what do you do?
o: pass by. it's not your people, and not your problem.
stop, bandage him, and pay for his care.
go and find someone from his own people to help.
games.why: he had compassion on him: oil and wine on the wounds, his own animal, an inn, and money for more. the hero comes from across the line.

practice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let a breath out. Think back over this week and find one moment when someone needed something and you passed by on the other side: a text you didn't answer, a coworker who looked lost.
No need to judge yourself. Everyone passes by sometimes. Just see the moment clearly, and picture what stopping would have looked like.
If you pray, you can hold that person in prayer. If you don't, hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: The Good Samaritan. The man from across the line who stopped, and turned the question from who counts to who acts. Twelfth word.

carryVoice: Your line: the neighbor is whoever is in front of you. Not who's close. Who's there. That's day twelve.
